notes: New pages are stored on cdn.hzrd149.com and nostr.download. The second default used to be blossom.primal.net, which labels stylesheets as plain text, and a browser will not use a stylesheet labelled that way, so a page fetched from it could show up without its design. Pages published before keep the servers they were published with.

Your page could appear without its design, as plain text and oversized pictures, when it was opened through a gateway that fetched its stylesheet from one particular storage server. That server guessed what kind of file the stylesheet was from a comment inside it and guessed wrong, and browsers refuse to use a stylesheet labelled as a web page. The stylesheet and the toolbar script no longer confuse it. Taking this upgrade fixes a page that sometimes looked broken.

Paying for AI credit is safer. If the page closed or the connection dropped while your payment was being collected, the coins could be left stranded. What is needed to finish is now saved first, and Check payment picks up the same payment again rather than asking you to pay twice.
Adding AI credit now has a window of its own: choose an amount, pay, and carry on where you were. Before you ask for anything, you see your balance and a rough idea of what the request will cost.

A preview you paid for is no longer thrown away when a follow-up request fails. You can ask for further changes to a proposed page, go back to earlier versions, and compare it with the page as it is before keeping it. A draft also comes back after a reload.

Rewriting the whole page with AI now keeps your live feeds of posts exactly as they were. Before, a redesign could quietly remove them. A rewrite that leaves one out is not used, and you are told why.
A preview can no longer overwrite changes you made while the AI was working, and going back to your instruction keeps what you wrote.
Your AI provider, address and model are saved together with your key on your relays, so another device picks up the same setup.
Dialogs keep keyboard focus inside them and announce what they are doing to screen readers.

A page built from a description now always arrives with a design of its own. The instructions the writing model was given listed the things the publisher adds to your page for you, and some models read that list as covering the look of the page too, so they wrote the words and left the styling to somebody who was never going to supply it. What came out was a wall of plain text with no colours, no spacing and no layout, and nothing on screen said why. It is now told plainly that the design is the page's own work and that nothing else provides one, and a page that still turns up without a stylesheet is refused and offered again rather than published as it is.

Asking to change a page no longer risks losing the look of it. A rewrite could come back with the right words in a page stripped of its styling, for the same reason, and the page you were shown afterwards was your writing with the design gone. Keeping the page as it was now explicitly includes keeping what makes it look like itself.

A page no longer loses its whole design over a single character. Quotation marks, dashes and other symbols are often written inside a stylesheet as a short code starting with a backslash, and the check that stops a page quietly fetching things from other people's servers treated every one of those as an attempt to do exactly that, and threw the entire stylesheet away without a word. That check now reads a stylesheet the way a browser does, so ordinary symbols are left alone, while a page that really does reach out to another server is still stopped, and stopped in a couple of cases it used to miss.

Asking AI to change your page no longer deletes the photographs you uploaded. It was told to write pages with their pictures missing, which is right when it is building a page it has no photographs for, and wrong when it is rewriting one where you have already put them in. Your pictures now come back with the page, matched up even when the rewrite changes everything written around them.
The preview of a rewritten page no longer has the toolbar's own words printed under it, and it now loads your page's stylesheet, so what you are shown is what you will get.

A picture is now changed by clicking it, like everything else on your page. Click an empty photo frame, or a photo you want to replace, and the picker opens: a file from your computer or phone, cropped to the shape of the space before it is uploaded, or one of the pictures already on your site. Until now pictures were the one kind of content that did not respond to being clicked, and the only way in was a button called Edit content that says nothing about pictures.
While you are editing, a picture shows that it can be clicked. The toolbar's own pictures, and pictures other people posted into a feed, stay as they are.
The content form still lists every picture, and both ways lead to the same place.

The Copy button under a newly made key works, and tells the truth. It used to say Copied whether or not anything had been copied, had no second way to try on browsers that do not offer the first, and never changed back, so it looked like a button that had stopped working. It now says Copied for three seconds and returns to Copy, and if it genuinely cannot reach the clipboard it says so and tells you to select the key instead. The key is on screen the whole time either way.

Asking AI to build a page no longer stops half way through writing it. The model was given a fixed amount of room, and nothing about a description tells you how long the page will turn out, so a page that ran past it was cut off mid-sentence and thrown away. It now asks for as much room as there is, and steps down only if the model it is talking to says that is more than it allows.

When a reply does stop early, the message says which thing stopped it and what to do about that particular thing. One sentence used to cover every case and told you to try a smaller change, which is no help at all when you were asking for a page to be built in the first place.

Setting up Simple setup is quicker. Your AI credit and the half that supports nsite-clay are two errands at two different places, and they were run one after the other while you waited for the first. They now go at once, so the wait is the longer of the two rather than both added together. Neither can be lost: both halves are written down before either is sent.

Choosing a picture now crops it to the shape of the space it is going into, without being asked. The page knows how wide and how tall that space is, so the frame starts as the right shape and a photograph from a phone stops stretching the layout or being chopped about by the browser.

The shape can be changed in the crop window itself, with the photograph in front of you. It used to be a dropdown you filled in before choosing a file, which is the one moment nobody can judge it, and changing your mind meant starting again.

Pictures on a page built by AI can now be changed. Every image gets a row in the content form with a Choose a picture button, which uploads a file from your computer or your phone, crops it to the shape the layout wants first, and can also use a picture already on your site. Before, the page had places for photographs and no way to put one in without editing HTML.

A page is asked for with its photographs missing rather than invented. An image with no file behind it now draws itself as a dashed frame with a description of what belongs there, so the layout is right from the start, the gap is obviously a gap, and the content form has the row that fills it. Nothing is ever pointed at a stock photo service that could disappear.
If you already have a page with pictures that cannot be changed, ask the AI to change anything on it and the picture rows appear with the rest.

Credit you buy from inside your own page is now saved to your relays by itself, encrypted to your key, the same as the credit you bought when you published. Before, a top-up bought here stayed in this one browser, and the next device you opened the page on found nothing.

Saving to your relays several times in a row now works. A note that replaces an older one is ignored if both claim the same second, so one of three writes made moments apart could be dropped while reporting that it had worked. Buying credit writes three times, so this was the write that mattered.

Taking an update no longer leaves you pressing Reload. The page waits for your gateway to start serving the new copy, which takes anything from seconds to a minute, and then reloads into it by itself. You can stop it if you would rather stay where you are, and it never does this over unsaved work.

Your AI credit is now found the moment you sign in to edit, rather than when you open the box that spends it. Before, the first thing you saw was a line saying you had no credit, corrected a second later, which is how a page holding your money reads as a page that is not.
Once found, the credit stays in this browser, so looking for it on your relays happens once here rather than before every edit.
The settings box now opens with the key you already own in it, instead of an empty field next to a button offering to fetch it.

Signing in with a remote signer now asks for everything it will need while you are pairing, including permission to read your own encrypted notes back. Without that, the signer asked again later, in the middle of something else.

The preview of a rewritten page shows the new page only. The page you have is behind the dialog already, and showing it twice pushed the button that accepts the change off the bottom of the screen. Dialogs now keep their buttons in view however tall the thing inside them is.

Edit with AI now means the whole page. Ask for a darker design, a new section, the photos moved, or all three at once, and you get a preview of the whole page next to the one you have before anything changes. It used to quietly rewrite whichever paragraph you had last clicked, which was both a surprise and the smaller half of what people wanted. That paragraph is still there as a choice in the box, next to the page.
Nothing a rewrite does is published until you press Save, and one undo brings the old page back, exactly as with any other edit.

The credit you paid for now follows you to your own page. It is bought in the publisher and spent in the page, and those are two different addresses as far as a browser is concerned, so the page used to tell you that you had no credit while your money sat there untouched. It now looks on your own relays, where the key was saved, and finds it.

A preview you are not happy with is no longer a dead end. You can say what should be different about it and get that change without describing the page again from nothing, or go back to your description and edit what you wrote. Both are on the screen next to Use this page.

The screen where a new page begins now shows its two routes as two routes. Describing a page for AI to build and starting from a finished page each carry their own heading and their own explanation, so the sentence about the twelve free templates can no longer be read as a description of the AI form above it.
After you pay for Simple setup, the button with the price on it goes away and the page starts building what you described, instead of offering to sell you the same thing again.

Your AI credit is no longer trapped in one browser. It is saved to your own Nostr relays, encrypted so that only your key can read it, and any device you can sign in on gets it back. Downloading a copy is still there for when relays are unreachable, but it is no longer the only way to keep what you paid for.

Taking unspent credit back is now a matter of typing your Lightning address. The node pays it there. If you would rather have a Cashu token to paste into a wallet, leave the address empty and you still get one.

The AI settings box no longer asks you to fill in a key you do not have yet. With our node the key arrives when you pay, so the field says so, and the buttons that ask the node about a balance stay switched off until there is one to ask about. Pressing them used to show a raw error code.

Setting up AI when you publish is now one button with the price on it. It takes one Lightning payment, half of which supports nsite-clay and half of which becomes your own credit, and sets everything up for you. The old settings box is still there behind a link for anyone who wants another provider or their own API key.

Your pages load faster for everyone who is only reading them. The part that keeps your file's own formatting when you save needs an HTML parser, and that parser was a third of everything a visitor had to download before your page appeared. It now waits until you sign in to edit, so a reader never downloads it at all and the rest arrives sooner.

Nothing about saving changes. When you edit, it is fetched in the background while you work, and your save keeps your formatting exactly as before. On the rare occasion it cannot be reached, the page still saves; it just rewrites the formatting, which is what it did before this feature existed.

When you ask AI for a new page, the page now starts with your own words. The AI sometimes wrote a sentence introducing itself at the top, left a stray line of punctuation behind it, and pushed the page's title out of place; all of that is gone.

On a page AI built for you, the facts in a table or a list can be changed. Opening hours, prices, a list of what to bring: these are now editable on the page and they appear in the content form, where before they were the one thing you could never correct.
A long answer from AI is no longer cut off. Pages that take a few minutes to write now finish, and an AI that has genuinely stopped replying is reported sooner, in a sentence that says what happened.
Keeping an AI edit no longer leaves an invisible mark in your saved file. It was harmless to read, but it built up with every edit and made the file look changed when it was not.
The publisher no longer tells the AI service who you are. It sends the description you wrote and the template you picked, and nothing else.

The publisher now speaks Spanish, Slovak and Czech the whole way through. The messages it shows while your site goes out, and the warning that a page already exists where you are publishing, used to appear in English whatever language you had chosen.
AI says it has no credit before you write anything, rather than after you have described the page you wanted and waited for it.
The counter moves while AI is thinking. Some models spend the first minute working out what to write before writing a word, and a counter sitting at zero for that long looked broken.
When AI offers to change something, you see what is on the page now next to what would replace it. Deciding whether the new wording is better should not be a memory test.

You can now ask AI for a page. In the publisher, open the AI section, describe what you want and look at the result before anything is published; you can start from nothing or from a template. AI runs through our own Routstr node by default and is paid with Cashu or Lightning, and its settings let you choose another node or model, or your own API key.

On a page you already have, click the words or the block you want changed and choose Edit with AI. The result appears as a preview and nothing changes until you keep it. Undo takes an accepted change back, and Save publishes it.

Undo and Redo now sit on the editing bar, so a block you deleted by mistake comes back with its buttons still working. The history lasts for the editing session; your published versions stay in History as before.
Choosing a picture has a crop step now. Pick free, square, wide or 4:3 before the file is uploaded, and only the crop you accept is stored.

The content form learns new field types from the page itself: a date picker, a dropdown, a number field, and a field where you can write with links, lists and bold text. A page that has not been told about them looks exactly as it did.

Saving keeps more of your file as you wrote it. A small change no longer rewrites the punctuation and spacing of the whole document when it does not have to, so the file stays recognisable in a text editor. When that cannot be done safely, the save falls back to exactly what it did before.

The things a page repeats, the events in a list or the cards in a row, can carry the same small strip of buttons the page's blocks already carry: move it, copy it, delete it, in one place with one meaning rather than a different row of words for each kind of thing. It comes with the stylesheet, so a page built from one of the newer templates has it and needs nothing set up. Nothing on a page already published changes, because the buttons it was built with are its own markup and no update rewrites those.

The list of what changed in an update is readable now. Every line arrived cut off mid-word with a sideways scrollbar under it, so the one thing this dialog exists to show you was the one thing you could not read.

Taking an update no longer reloads the page out from under you. It says the newer version is on your site and leaves the reload to you, so you stay signed in and whatever else was on the screen stays there.

A page you have already updated stops asking you to update it again. For a few minutes after you publish, a gateway can still hand out the copy of your page it had before, and that older copy would offer you the same update a second time. It now says the update is published and offers you a reload.
Updating no longer answers you with a list of dead links. Those are about your own pages, they were there before you pressed Update, and you will hear about them the next time you save.

The toolbar speaks the language of the page. On a Slovak, Czech or Spanish page, Write, Edit content, Settings, History and Save stayed in English beside the words that had been translated. A button you renamed yourself is left as you wrote it.

The sign-in box, the settings, the version list and this update offer come out as boxes again on a page whose own stylesheet has a rule about forms. On one site this dialog arrived as four narrow columns with its buttons pushed off the side of the screen, which made it almost impossible to read and nearly impossible to press. The content panel had the same problem on a page that styles its asides.
The box you paste a key into is now as wide as the dialog around it, rather than the small default the browser picks.

A link to a page that is not in your site no longer stops you saving. The page is published, and a panel lists the addresses that lead nowhere and stays on the screen until you close it, with a button that copies the list. Until now one link to a page that did not exist yet meant nothing could be saved at all.
A link written as /shop/ is understood to mean the page at /shop/index.html, the way any web address works, so a site with more than one page stops reporting its own links as broken.

When a save fails, the reason stays on the screen until you dismiss it and can be selected and copied. It used to vanish after two seconds, which is not long enough to read a list of file names, let alone send one to whoever can fix it.
A page that carries no content form no longer shows an Edit content button that opens nothing.
Pasting into a one-line region no longer splits it. A pasted paragraph used to nest a second <a> inside a button, which came back after the next load as two buttons with the first one empty.
A block's rail can reach inside the block. The new ⌷ button lists what a block is made of, so a stray element can be removed without deleting the block around it.
A button's link can be changed. Pressing the link button inside one used to try to put a link inside a link.
Settings says which runtime the page is running, and can move it to a newer one.
A dialog opened on top of another no longer shares its Escape key with the one underneath.

A publish that stalls now ends and says which Blossom server stopped answering, instead of sitting on "Uploading… 1/4" forever. Every network call has a timeout, and each server gets its own line with a running clock.
A blob is signed once rather than once per base64 encoding, which halves how many times a phone signer asks you to approve the same upload.
The publisher has a panel for the relays and Blossom servers it uses, so one server refusing you is something you can work around without a terminal.

A publish asks the Blossom servers what they already hold before it signs anything, so a phone signer is asked once per file rather than once per file per server, all in one burst at the start. Republishing an unchanged site now needs no upload approvals at all.
nc:watch-dom, off by default, makes any change to the page count as an edit rather than only typing.
